newsitem.title: USA: Clinton stretches lead after Mideast summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton stretches lead after Mideast summit.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Clinton hit the campaign trail again on Thursday after a Middle East summit gave him a boost in the polls against Republican Bob Dole.
Clinton wooed voters in western New York state before going into seclusion to prepare for Sunday's presidential debate, the first of two he will hold against Dole in the next two weeks.

In the latest Reuters tracking poll, conducted by John Zogby Group, Clinton led by 46.2 percent to Dole's 32.9 percent. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot trailed with 4.6 percent. The margin of error was plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.
The result represented an improvement of 2.7 percentage points for Clinton in the past 24 hours and the president's best rating since the daily poll began on Tuesday. The election is Nov. 5.
Clinton dominated the headlines in the past two days by hosting a Middle East summit that produced an agreement by Israel and the Palestinians to resume peace talks but no substantive progress.
"Stated simply, Bill Clinton had a huge day on Tuesday, probably as a result of all the publicity surrounding the Middle East summit," said pollster John Zogby.
Dole criticized Clinton for conducting "photo-op diplomacy" but found it difficult to make his voice heard.
The Republican nominee was campaigning on Thursday in Tennessee and Georgia before heading to his south Florida condominium to complete his own debate preparation.

In Johnson City, Tennessee, Dole blasted Clinton's foreign policy as "ruddlerless and illusionary" and suggested that he may have convened the inconclusive Israeli-Palestinian summit to promote his re-election.

"In the last three years you and I have seen a series of photo opportunities, treaty signings, staged handshakes and even military theatrics -- all designed to create the impression of foreign policy progress," Dole told a meeting of businessmen in this east Tennesssee city.
Speaking about the Middle East summit, Dole added: "Frankly it is unclear what President Clinton expected out of a such a meeting. Some have suggested he may have had November 5 on his mind."
Clinton also released a new campaign ad touting his initiatives to promote youth curfews and school uniforms, both centrist themes popular with voters.
Before leaving Washington, the president signed three crime-related bills, including one requiring the FBI to keep track of violent sex offenders.

"This is a good day for America because we have seen a sea change in the attitudes of our people, the actions of communities and the work in Washington on the problem of crime," Clinton said during a Rose Garden ceremony.
At a rally at Buffalo airport attended by several thousand cheering supporters Clinton previewed some of the themes he was expected to emphasize in his showdown with Dole.
Clinton said that when he ran for president in 1992 "we were drifting toward the 21st Century" and "four years later, we're on the right track roaring toward the 21st Century."

After the rally Clinton flew by helicopter to the renowned Chautauqua Institution, a gated Victorian village founded more than a century ago as a vacation retreat for Methodist Sunday School teachers.
It was to be his training camp for the televised campaign debate scheduled to occur in Hartford, Conn.

Campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart told reporters Clinton, who is famed for his oratorical skills, was "slightly apprehensive at this point" because Dole prepped for the debate while Clinton tried to end the violence between Israelis and Palestinians that erupted last week.
Dole said he would win the debate simply by showing up because Clinton was such a good debater.
Sunday's debate was scheduled to be followed by a vice presidential showdown between Kemp and Al Gore on Wednesday and a second Clinton-Dole debate Oct. 16.
